key_moments.situation: This is an interesting beginning of the session, because the tutor specifically asks the student to get through as many problems as they can and tells the student to ask for help if they need help.  Then, when the student asks for help, the tutor just tells them to skip the problem.  I wonder if the tutor was concerned about taking up time out of the 20 minutes to explain the problems that the student needed support on.  If that's the case, the tutor should have just said, "If there is a problem you are not sure how to solve, either take an educated guess or skip it."  It seems like the tutor is avoiding the more rigorous parts of the problem set.  Also, since the tutor didn't check the student's answers, now the tutor doesn't know how the student did on this problem set other than having trouble with problems 9 and 14.  If the tutor knows that the student is struggling, it would make sense for the tutor to find out which problems the student did well on and which ones the student needs support with.
key_moments.action: I did not see a particular strategy used to push for rigor, but the tutor seemed to attempt to scaffold during lines 37-43.  The tutor did not seem to be pushing the student's thinking about the work yet.  The tutor gave the student the problem set and the time to work on it, and briefly checked in to see how far along the student was.  When the tutor addressed the student's hesitation on problem 14, the tutor gave very quick and minimal guidance that reminded the student of a rule but didn't necessarily help the student with their misconception in an effective way.  I am curious to know how the student has been working on topics like this previously because it seems that the student is taking extra time on problems that are relatively quick, and that the student needs more support on a few of the problems.
key_moments.result: The tutor's strategy does not seem to be effective yet because the tutor spends 20 minutes of the tutoring session on a very worthwhile problem set containing lots of important math concepts, and then does not review it at all to see how the student did.  It seems unusual to not gather the information from the student, especially if the student took longer than expected to complete the work and struggled on at least two problems that we know about.  Having taught 6th grade math before, I would be concerned about fact fluency and pace of work completion if it took a student 20 minutes to complete this particular problem set, unless there was a situation where the student had a processing or learning difference that prevented them from working at a typical pace.  These 15 problems could mostly be done with quick mental math, so I was surprised to see the student took the full 20 minutes.  It seems like it would be well worth the tutor's and student's time to take a few minutes to review the problems, have the student explain their thinking, and reteach concepts that the student needed help with.  However, it is important to note that the tutor immediately goes into a well-scaffolded lesson on what algebra is, what variables are, and how to solve for a variable, so it seems that the tutor is addressing the student's misconceptions.  With that assistance, the student begins to demonstrate better understanding and quicker work completion.  I still think it would be worthwhile for the tutor to see how the student did on these 15 problems so that the tutor will know which concepts they need to review and/or reteach with the student.

I'm interested to see whether the student will choose to update their avatar at some point during this lesson.  Overall, I think this strategy was an effective one, especially for a hesitant student, because it gives them an outlet to engage but doesn't push them to do so if they don't feel comfortable yet.
